notes.b: Rhythmic gymnastics is an aesthetic activity, meaning one judged on how it looks and feels as well as on what is done. It joins the movement of dance with the skilful handling of a small hand-held object.
points: It is a floor discipline that combines dance-like body movement with handling a piece of apparatus (the hand-held equipment used in the routine).
Routines are set to music, so the movement is planned to fit the sound rather than done in silence.
The apparatus used is a ball, hoop, ribbon, rope or club, and a routine is built around the chosen piece.
notes.tip: Rhythmic gymnastics is used as an aesthetic activity in written answers, so be ready to link it to aesthetic criteria, music and choreography (the planning of the movements). Keep it separate from artistic gymnastics: do not bring in vaults or tumbling.

notes.b: Balances and pivots are the basic body skills of the floor sequence. In a balance the performer stays still, and in a pivot the performer turns while keeping a set shape.
points: Balance: the performer stands on one foot on relevé, meaning raised up on the toes, with the free leg (the one off the floor) held in a clear shape.
The balance is held still, because a wobble or movement during the hold shows a loss of control.
Pivot: the performer turns on one foot, on the ball of the foot (the padded part just behind the toes), with a fixed body shape held through the turn.
Holding the shape during the pivot means the body does not change position mid-turn, which makes the turn look controlled.

notes.b: Rolls and splits are floor skills that show control and range of movement. Rolls travel along the body or floor, while splits show how far the legs can open.
points: Body rolls: controlled rolls of the body on the floor, with the performer in charge of the speed and direction rather than simply tumbling.
Rolling can also be done with the apparatus, which is rolled along the body or the floor, as the ball and hoop blocks below show.
Front splits (one leg forward, one back) and side splits (legs out to each side) are performed on the floor or in the air.

notes.b: Hops, leaps and skips carry the performer across the floor. They are the travelling movements of the sequence, and they are judged on the shape made in the air and on the landing.
points: These are travelling movements with a clear shape held in the air, so the body looks deliberate and not loose while off the ground.
A split leap, with the legs at maximum range (as far apart as they will go), is an example.
Each one finishes with a soft landing, which keeps the movement controlled and quiet.

notes.h: Body waves, bends, circles, swings and turns
notes.b: These movements link the other skills together and make a routine look fluid. They use the whole body rather than just a limb.
points: These are flowing movements through the whole body, such as a wave travelling from one end of the body to the other.
They show flexibility (range of movement at the joints) and fluency (smooth, unbroken movement).

notes.b: The ball is handled by rolling, bouncing, throwing and catching. Every skill must look smooth, and the ball is never held tightly.
points: Rolls of the ball along the arms and along the floor.
Bounces of the ball on the floor.
Throws and catches with one hand, without gripping the ball, so the ball rests in the hand and is not clutched.

notes.b: The hoop is a ring that can roll, spin and be passed through, which gives a wider range of skills than the ball.
points: Rolls of the hoop along the floor.
Rotations of the hoop around the hand or body, meaning the hoop is spun in a circle.
Throws and catches of the hoop, and passing through the hoop, where the performer steps or moves through the ring.

notes.b: The ribbon is a long strip of cloth on a stick, and it makes its shapes in the air. Its rule is different from the other apparatus: it must never stop.
points: Continuous patterns such as spirals, snakes (wave shapes) and circles are drawn in the air.
The ribbon must stay in motion throughout, because the patterns are only seen while it is moving.
Stopping or knotting the ribbon is a fault, meaning a mistake that is penalised.
notes.tip: If asked about the ribbon, state that it must keep moving and that stopping or knotting it is a fault.

notes.b: The rope is used for skipping and jumping as well as swinging, throwing and catching.
points: Skips and jumps through the rope.
Swings and circles of the rope.
Throws and catches of the rope.

notes.b: Clubs are held one in each hand, so they are used in pairs. The work is mainly small, rhythmic movement.
points: Mills: small circles made with the clubs.
Swings with the clubs.
Tapping with the clubs, which also makes a sound that can be matched to the music.
Throws and catches of one or both clubs.

notes.b: In rhythmic gymnastics the music shapes the movement. The routine is made to fit the music, which is what makes it aesthetic.
points: Movements are matched to the tempo (the speed) of the music, so fast music gets quick movements and slow music gets slower ones.
Movements are matched to the phrasing (the way the music is grouped into musical sentences) and accents (the stressed beats) of the music.
The routine reflects the mood of the music, for example a calm piece would be expressed with gentle, flowing movement.
notes.tip: When asked about music and choreography, give all three links: tempo, phrasing and accents, and mood.

notes.b: Composing means planning the routine so that it is a complete piece and not a string of separate skills. Each part below makes the whole routine more interesting to watch.
points: The routine has a start position and an end position, so it has a clear beginning and finish.
It uses a variety of body groups (types of body movement, such as balances, pivots, leaps and waves) and apparatus elements (the handling skills), so it does not repeat itself.
Space and levels are used throughout, meaning the performer moves across the floor and works at different heights, from low to high.
Links between elements flow smoothly, so one skill leads into the next without stopping.
Body work and apparatus work are coordinated with each other, so the body and the equipment move together.
notes.tip: Rhythmic gymnastics is used as an aesthetic activity in written answers, so use these composition points as aesthetic criteria.

notes.b: A routine is judged on three things: how hard it is, how well it is carried out, and how artistic it is.
points: Difficulty: body and apparatus elements are scored for difficulty, so harder skills are worth more.
Execution: deductions (marks taken off) are made for loss of balance, dropped apparatus and poor technique.
Artistry: music, expression and composition are judged, so the way the routine is put together and performed counts as well as the skills.

notes.b: Rhythmic gymnastics asks for a mix of physical and mental qualities, because the performer must move well, handle the apparatus and stay in time with the music.
points: Flexibility and balance are both required, for splits, leaps and held balances.
Hand-eye co-ordination (using the eyes to guide the hands) is needed to handle the apparatus, for example to catch a thrown ball or hoop.
Muscular endurance (the ability of muscles to keep working without tiring) is needed to sustain the routine.
Rhythm and timing match the movements to the music.
Concentration is needed throughout the routine, so that errors such as a dropped apparatus are avoided.

notes.b: The performer moves quickly, stretches far and throws equipment into the air. Safety steps reduce the risk of injury and accidents.
points: Warm-up includes flexibility preparation, so the muscles and joints are ready for stretching skills such as splits.
Performers need adequate space between them, so that they and their apparatus do not collide.
A suitable floor surface is used.
The condition of the apparatus is checked before use.

keyTerms.definition: A floor discipline combining dance-like body movement with handling a piece of apparatus, performed to music.
Rising onto the toes or the ball of the foot with the heel lifted.
A turn on one foot on the ball of the foot, with a fixed body shape.
A leap in which the legs are held at maximum range in a split shape in the air.
A small circle made with a club.
A flowing movement that travels through the whole body.
A hand-held object used in a routine: a ball, hoop, ribbon, rope or club.
The way music is grouped into shaped sections called phrases.
A beat or note in the music that is emphasised.

factCards.definition: Ball, hoop, ribbon, rope and club.
Balances, pivots, rolls, splits, hops, leaps and skips, and body waves, bends, circles, swings and turns.

factCards.term: Ribbon: what it must never do
factCards.definition: Stop or knot. It stays in continuous motion through patterns such as spirals, snakes and circles.
Mills, swings, tapping, and throws and catches of one or both clubs.
Difficulty of body and apparatus elements; execution, reduced for loss of balance, dropped apparatus and poor technique; artistry through music, expression and composition.

questions.prompt: Describe how a rhythmic gymnast combines body movement and apparatus handling in a routine set to music.
questions.model: A rhythmic gymnast performs a routine to music, combining body movement with apparatus handling throughout. The body movement groups are balances on relevé, pivots, rolls, splits, hops, leaps and skips, and body waves, bends, circles, swings and turns. These are linked with apparatus skills, for example a split leap performed while a ball is rolled along the arm, or a hoop rotated around the hand during a balance. The routine starts and ends in set positions, the links between elements flow, and the body work and apparatus work are coordinated with each other. Movements are matched to the tempo, phrasing and accents of the music, and the routine reflects its mood. Judging covers the difficulty of the body and apparatus elements, deductions for loss of balance, dropped apparatus and poor technique, and artistry through music, expression and composition.

questions.prompt: Name three pieces of rhythmic gymnastics apparatus and one skill performed with each.
questions.model: Ball: a throw and catch with one hand, without gripping the ball. Hoop: a rotation around the hand or body. Ribbon: a continuous spiral, kept in motion without stopping or knotting.
